title: Hosea 11:1–12
context: Hosea 11:1–12 is the LORD speaking as a loving parent. When Israel was a child he loved him and called his son out of Egypt, taught Ephraim to walk, healed them, and drew them with cords of love, though they kept turning to the Baals. Matthew 2:15 applies 11:1 to Jesus’ return from Egypt; that use is named here alongside Hosea’s own meaning, the exodus of Israel, without merging the two, and the Matthew 2:15 box discusses it. Because they refused to return, the sword will fall on their cities and Assyria will rule them. Yet the LORD cries, "How can I give you up, Ephraim?" He will not make them like Admah and Zeboiim, cities destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23); his compassion is stirred, and he will not carry out his fierce anger, for he is God and not man, the Holy One among them. The LORD will roar like a lion, and his children will come trembling from the west, from Egypt, and from Assyria, and he will settle them in their homes. Questions about God’s relenting are discussed in the 1 Samuel 15:29 and Judges 10:16 boxes; shared ground: both traditions receive 11:8–9 as a revelation of God’s covenant compassion. Versification: English 11:12 is Hebrew 12:1, and English 12:1–14 is Hebrew 12:2–15; this page keeps the WEB numbers.

verses.text: “When Israel was a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says that when Israel was a child he loved him and called his son out of Egypt. Arminian readers see God’s love as the foundation of Israel’s existence, and they receive Matthew 2:15 as showing Christ embodying Israel’s story while inviting trust in God’s faithful care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the exodus as an act of God’s electing love, and they read Matthew’s use as typological providence fulfilled in Christ. Both traditions name Hosea’s meaning and Matthew’s use without merging them, and the Matthew 2:15 box discusses the difference in emphasis.

verses.text: They called to them, so they went from them. They sacrificed to the Baals, and burned incense to engraved images.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the more they were called, the more they went away, sacrificing to the Baals and burning incense to images. Arminians see God’s persistent calling met with persistent refusal, which shows the reality of human rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the depth of human sin in turning from God’s love. Both traditions note that some read they called as the prophets calling Israel, and they read the verse as a lament.

verses.text: Yet I taught Ephraim to walk. I took them by their arms, but they didn’t know that I healed them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he taught Ephraim to walk, took them in his arms, but they did not know he healed them. Arminian readers see a tender picture of God’s care, like a parent teaching a child to walk.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s gracious care in Israel’s history. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and see the tragedy that Israel did not recognize God’s healing.

verses.text: I drew them with cords of a man, with ties of love; and I was to them like those who lift up the yoke on their necks; and I bent down to him and I fed him.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he drew them with cords of a man and ties of love, lifted the yoke from their necks, and bent down to feed them. Arminians see God’s love drawing his people gently, not by force, which they believe reflects how grace works.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s love as effective and tender. Both traditions hold the picture of God’s gentle care as shared ground, while differing in how they describe the way his drawing works in individuals (compare John 6:44 by reference).

verses.text: “They won’t return into the land of Egypt; but the Assyrian will be their king, because they refused to repent.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they will not return to Egypt, but Assyria will be their king, because they refused to repent. Arminian readers see judgment following the people’s refusal to return to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty over the outcome. Both traditions note that 8:13 and 9:3 speak of returning to Egypt, and some read this verse as a question; they name the difference without forcing a single explanation.

verses.text: The sword will fall on their cities, and will destroy the bars of their gates, and will put an end to their plans.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the sword will fall on their cities, destroy their gates, and end their plans. Arminians see the consequences of refusing God, as their own schemes come to nothing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s judgment on human plans. Both traditions read the verse as describing the Assyrian invasion, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: My people are determined to turn from me. Though they call to the Most High, he certainly won’t exalt them.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says his people are determined to turn from him, and though they call to the Most High, he will not exalt them. Arminian readers see a settled resistance that does not respond to God’s calls.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the bent of the human heart away from God. Both traditions note that the verse is difficult in Hebrew and translated in different ways, and they hold its details loosely.

verses.text: “How can I give you up, Ephraim? How can I hand you over, Israel? How can I make you like Admah? How can I make you like Zeboiim? My heart is turned within me, my compassion is aroused.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks how he can give Ephraim up or make them like Admah and Zeboiim, for his heart is turned and his compassion aroused. Arminians see God’s deep compassion, which holds back the full judgment the people deserve.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s covenant love as stronger than Israel’s sin. Both traditions note that Admah and Zeboiim were destroyed with Sodom (Deuteronomy 29:23), and they hold this as shared ground about God’s compassion.

verses.text: I will not execute the fierceness of my anger. I will not return to destroy Ephraim, for I am God, and not man—the Holy One among you. I will not come in wrath.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will not carry out his fierce anger or destroy Ephraim, for he is God and not man, the Holy One among them. Arminian readers see God’s holiness expressed in mercy, so that his compassion is not human weakness but divine faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s unchanging covenant purpose. Questions about God’s relenting are discussed in the 1 Samuel 15:29 and Judges 10:16 boxes; shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a revelation of God’s compassion.

verses.text: They will walk after the LORD, who will roar like a lion; for he will roar, and the children will come trembling from the west.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they will walk after him as he roars like a lion, and his children will come trembling from the west. Arminians see God calling his people back with power, and their trembling as reverent response.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the roar as God’s sovereign call that gathers his people. Both traditions note that the lion’s roar elsewhere signals judgment (5:14), but here it calls the children home.

verses.text: They will come trembling like a bird out of Egypt, and like a dove out of the land of Assyria; and I will settle them in their houses,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says they will come trembling like birds from Egypt and doves from Assyria, and he will settle them in their homes. Arminian readers see the promise of return from exile, showing that God’s compassion leads to restoration.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s faithfulness to restore his people. Both traditions hold this as shared ground, and they note that the dove image recalls 7:11, now turned from folly to homecoming.

verses.text: Ephraim surrounds me with falsehood, and the house of Israel with deceit. Judah still strays from God, and is unfaithful to the Holy One.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Ephraim surrounds him with lies and Israel with deceit, and Judah still strays from God. Arminians see the sad reality that the people’s unfaithfulness continues even after God’s compassionate words.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as transitioning to the charges of chapter 12. Both traditions note that this verse is numbered 12:1 in Hebrew, and that its last line about Judah is read in different ways.
